This would show that no single min_distance/footprint setting puts every family within 10%.
review_reason: The run never executed. The evaluator rejected the params with 'ValueError: unknown params [overlay]', after 0.02 s. There are no metrics, no by_family medians and no overlay images, so the hypothesis cannot be tested in either direction. That hypothesis was pooled max_rel_error >= 0.10, with columnar and elongated over-counting easing to 10–30% and fine_equiaxed and equiaxed_single swinging to under-counting. Nothing can be said about merged grains, over-split grains, scratches or pores taken as boundaries, or missed boundaries, because no segmentation was produced. The failure is a plumbing error, not a scientific result. 'overlay' was placed inside params_json, but the method's allowed keys are only boundary, denoise, exclude_edge, fill_boundaries, footprint, line_width_px, min_area_px, min_distance and sigma. The evidence therefore neither supports nor refutes the claim that no single isotropic min_distance/footprint setting puts every family within 10%; my confidence in any conclusion from this iteration is 0%. Two issues with the plan itself remain. First, the registered decision rule is pooled max_rel_error >= 0.10, but the hypothesis is about per-family medians. A pooled value >= 0.10 could come from one family failing badly, not the predicted two-way split, so the family-level predictions must be checked against by_family in execute.json, not the pooled number. Second, the plan's prior of about 60% is a judgement and is not yet backed by data.

rationale:
Iteration 2 left an unresolved tradeoff. At min_distance=14, columnar over-counted by 51% and elongated by 38%, while fine_equiaxed had already started to under-count by 2–7.5%. The research question needs to know whether this isotropic marker-spacing method can reach 10% on every morphology. I cannot write the h-maxima or interior-component marker method in this step, so the most useful experiment is to map the far side of the tradeoff with the same pipeline.

Only the marker-spacing knobs change. sigma=2, tophat line_width_px=4, min_area_px=80, exclude_edge=false and fill_boundaries=true are all held fixed, so the shift in each family's bias can be attributed to spacing alone.

The pooled max_rel_error averages over families and hides the failures that matter, so I will judge the outcome mainly on by_family medians in execute.json. The registered decision rule is pooled max_rel_error >= 0.10. If it stays below 0.10 and every family is within 10%, the hypothesis is falsified and parameter tuning is enough after all. I give that about 10%.

My expectation is that the hypothesis holds, at about 60% confidence. The doubtful part is how far the columnar and elongated errors fall: a 4:1 ridge about 60 px long could still carry 2–3 markers at a spacing of 22.

If the hypothesis holds, iterations 2 and 3 together bracket the isotropic optimum, and the conclusion is plain: the current method cannot meet the 10% target across morphologies. The next method to write would use interior-component markers, taken from connected non-boundary regions of the thresholded top-hat map, with h-maxima on the distance transform as the fallback. It should also reject scratches by filtering long straight boundary segments, and reject pores and rings by circularity and intensity.

I am making no noise-degradation claim yet. Corruption level is confounded with family, so any noise trend must be read within one family using by_family[f].by_level. The holdout split and the real 316L images stay untouched.
